newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end slightly up in listless trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end slightly up in listless trade.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed slightly higher in lackluster trade as players spent most of the day on the sidelines, waiting for the Federal Reserve policy-setting body's meeting on September 24, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended up 4/32 at 96-22/32. Its yield remained above the 7.0 percent psychological barrier at 7.02 percent.
Analysts said opinions appear to be fairly split on whether the Fed will raise interest rates or keep policy unchanged at the September Open Market Committee gathering.
Although they stressed it remains a very close call, most pundits said, however, the odds now seem to lean a little bit in favor of a tightening.
"The odds have tilted in the direction of a tightening," said Lee Youngdahl, economist and vice-president at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.

Analysts said recent comments by Federal Reserve officials on inflation and growth have, on average, cast a doubt on the market's expectations the central bank could keep policy on hold in Sepetember.
"It seems like the tradionally more dovish Fed members have put themselves now where they are willing to be led down that (tightening) path," Youngdahl said.
The economist added, however, he believed in a modest tightening of the federal funds rate, currently targeted at 5.25 percent. He did not expect the 5.0 percent discount rate to be changed.

Gary Thayer, senior economist at AG Edwards & Sons Inc, agreed. "Given some of (Fed) statements that have been released and the continued strength of the economy, we are probably going to see the Fed do something," he said.
"Probably a modest increase in rates," Thayer added.
Analysts said, however, the market paid little attention to comments by Fed vice-chairman Alice Rivlin on Wednesday, who said price stability in the U.S. is "doing very well."

Rivlin refused to make any further comments on the current state of the economy and on monetary policy. Fed officials usually refrain from talking about such issues when it gets close to an FOMC meeting.
On the economic indicator front, the market shrugged off the release of the U.S. international trade data for the month of July.

The report showed the U.S. trade deficit rose 42.6 percent to $11.68 billion against a revised June gap of $8.19 billion. The July gap was the biggest since a monthly average of $12.9 billion in the fourth quarter of 1987.
"The data show the economy was very strong recently...But it could also be a technical drag on third quarter growth," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed off five basis points at 5.12 percent. The six-month bill rate was down two points at 5.25 percent. The year bill rate fell two points to 5.51 percent.

The two-year note closed up 1/32 at 99-25/32, yielding 6.24 percent. The five-year note traded up 2/32 at 99-18/32 to yield 6.60 percent. The ten-year note closed up 2/32 at 101-8/32, yielding 6.82 percent.
